origin: Greek adiabatos, not to be passed through (by heat).

meanings.short: Happening without any heat flowing in or out.
meanings.long: A change is adiabatic when no heat enters or leaves, often because it is too quick for heat to flow, as in the compressions of a sound wave. A gas squeezed adiabatically warms up, so its pressure rises more than it would at constant temperature.

meanings.short: Changing slowly compared with the system's own natural motion, so the system can adjust smoothly as it goes.
meanings.long: In mechanics and quantum mechanics an adiabatic change is one made slowly compared with the period of the motion. Some quantities, the adiabatic invariants, then stay almost fixed, and a quantum system stays in the matching energy state.

meanings.short: Changing slowly compared with the system's own natural motion, so the system can adjust smoothly as it goes.
meanings.long: Here the change is slow compared with the period of the orbits, so certain quantities of each orbit stay almost fixed while the system slowly rearranges.

everyday: In everyday English to commute is to travel to work; in maths it means that the order does not matter.

meanings.short: Of two operations or matrices: to give the same result whichever is done first.
meanings.long: Two matrices A and B commute when AB equals BA. Ordinary numbers always commute under multiplication, but matrices and quantum operators often do not, and whether they do has physical consequences: in quantum mechanics, quantities whose operators commute can be measured together.

meanings.short: The difference AB minus BA of two matrices or operators; it is zero exactly when they commute.
meanings.long: The commutator is written [A, B] = AB − BA. It measures how far two operations fail to commute, and in quantum mechanics it decides which quantities can be known together.

everyday: Not a paper cover for letters: here, the outline of a wave.

meanings.short: The smooth curve that just touches the peaks of a fast oscillation or a row of peaks, showing how their size slowly changes.
meanings.long: When a fast oscillation has a slowly changing size, as in beats, a wave group or a damped vibration, the envelope is the outline traced by its peaks. In a wave group the envelope moves at the group velocity.

meanings.short: A particle that moves something from place to place, such as electric charge in a wire or semiconductor, or a force between other particles.
The fast oscillation inside a wave group or a radio signal, whose size the slow envelope changes.
meanings.long: Adding two waves of nearly equal frequency gives a fast wave at the average frequency, the carrier, inside a slowly varying envelope. In AM radio the carrier is the station's frequency and the envelope is the sound being sent.

meanings.short: A slow rise and fall in loudness or size when two oscillations of nearly equal frequency are added.
meanings.long: Two oscillations with frequencies close together add to one at the average frequency whose amplitude swells and fades. The swelling repeats at the difference of the two frequencies, the beat frequency, which is how musicians tune by ear.

meanings.short: The speed at which a group of waves, and the energy it carries, moves along.
meanings.long: A wave group built from waves of nearby wave numbers has an envelope that travels at dω/dk, the slope of the dispersion relation. It equals the phase velocity only when there is no dispersion.

meanings.short: The speed at which the crests of a single pure wave move: its angular frequency divided by its wave number.
meanings.long: For a wave of one wavelength, a crest moves at ω/k. In a dispersive medium this differs from the group velocity, so crests slide through a wave group as it travels.

meanings.short: The spreading out of a wave pulse because waves of different wavelengths travel at different speeds.
meanings.long: In a dispersive medium the phase velocity depends on wavelength, so the waves that make up a pulse drift apart and the pulse changes shape. A prism splitting white light into colours is the same effect.

meanings.short: The spread of the random speeds of stars, galaxies or particles about their average, measured as a standard deviation.
meanings.long: A velocity dispersion σ says how fast the members of a system move about at random; in a galaxy or cluster in balance it measures the depth of the gravitational well, and so the mass.

meanings.short: Short for the dispersion relation: how an excitation's energy depends on its wave number.
The rule that gives a wave's frequency for each wavelength, or wave number, in a particular medium.
meanings.long: Written ω(k), it holds all the information about how waves move in that medium: the phase velocity is ω/k and the group velocity dω/dk. When ω is simply proportional to k there is no dispersion.

meanings.short: Of a medium: carrying waves of every wavelength at the same speed, so a pulse keeps its shape as it travels.
meanings.long: In a non-dispersive medium the frequency is proportional to the wave number, so phase and group velocities are equal. Light in vacuum and waves on an ideal string are examples.

meanings.short: A condition that no longer changes with time, or for a driven system the lasting motion left once start-up effects die away.
meanings.long: A system driven by a steady or periodic input settles, after the transient has died out, into a motion set by the input alone, the steady state. More generally a steady state is one in which nothing changes with time even though things may flow through it.

meanings.short: Of the steady-state theory: a rival to the Big Bang in which the universe always looks the same, new matter appearing as it expands.
The part of a system's response that dies away with time, leaving only the steady state.
meanings.long: The transient depends on how the system was started; damping makes it shrink, usually exponentially. What remains afterwards is set by the input alone.

meanings.short: An ideal material whose charges move with no resistance at all, so no electric field can exist inside it.
meanings.long: Charges in a perfect conductor rearrange instantly to cancel any electric field that reaches them, so an electromagnetic wave is reflected completely. Good metals come close to this.

meanings.short: Patterns made by sand on a vibrating plate, which collects along the lines that do not move.
meanings.long: When a plate is made to vibrate at one of its normal-mode frequencies, sand is shaken off the moving parts and settles on the nodal lines, showing the shape of the mode.

meanings.short: The state of light in which the electric field keeps the same size and turns round in a circle as the wave goes past.
meanings.long: It is made of two equal perpendicular oscillations a quarter period apart. It can turn either way, clockwise or anticlockwise, as seen by someone facing the oncoming light.

meanings.short: The state of light in which the electric field traces out an ellipse as the wave goes past: the general case.
meanings.long: It arises when two perpendicular oscillations have unequal sizes, or a phase difference other than zero or a quarter period.

meanings.short: The state of light in which the electric field always points along one fixed line, swinging back and forth along it.
meanings.long: It is made of perpendicular oscillations that are in step (or exactly opposite). A polarizer passes only the part of the field along its easy axis.

meanings.short: Light whose field direction changes at random from moment to moment, so no direction is preferred.
meanings.long: Sunlight and light bulbs give unpolarized light: many atoms emit independently. A polarizer passes half of its intensity, whatever its angle.

meanings.short: A sharp bend or corner in a line or curve.
The bent stretch of field lines joining a charge's old and new field after a brief acceleration: a pulse of radiation.
meanings.long: Field lines far away still point to where the charge would have been, nearer ones to where it is; the kink joining them moves outward at the speed of light. Its sideways field is an electromagnetic wave, which is how accelerated charges radiate.

meanings.short: The Laser Interferometer Gravitational-wave Observatory: two large detectors in the United States that measure gravitational waves.
meanings.long: Each detector splits a laser beam along two arms 4 km long and compares their lengths to far less than the width of a proton. In 2015 LIGO made the first direct detection of gravitational waves, from two merging black holes.

everyday: Normal here means perpendicular, not usual.

meanings.short: A wave or ray hitting a surface head-on, along the line perpendicular to the surface.
A wave or ray striking a surface almost along it, at nearly 90 degrees from the perpendicular.
meanings.long: At grazing incidence almost all the light is reflected, which is why a distant lake or wet road shines so brightly.

meanings.short: The smallest angle between two point sources at which an instrument can still show them as two separate points.
meanings.long: Diffraction spreads each point into a small blur, so two points closer than about the wavelength divided by the aperture width merge into one. A larger lens or dish, or a shorter wavelength, gives finer resolution.

meanings.short: The smallest scale or mass that a computer simulation can represent; anything smaller is not followed.
The earlier moment at which a signal arriving now set out, earlier by its travel time at the speed of light.
meanings.long: The field at distance r and time t depends on what the source did at t − r/c, because changes in the field spread out at the speed of light.

meanings.short: Solving an equation by looking for a solution that is a sum of simpler functions, each depending on only one variable.
meanings.long: In Hamilton–Jacobi theory the characteristic function is tried as W = W₁(q₁) + W₂(q₂) + …, which splits the equation into separate ones, each set equal to a constant.

meanings.short: A wave pattern that stays in place, with points that never move (nodes) and points between them that swing the most.
meanings.long: A standing wave is the sum of two equal waves travelling in opposite directions. Every point oscillates in step, with a size that depends on position; on a string with fixed ends only certain wavelengths fit.

meanings.short: A wave whose shape moves along steadily in one direction.
meanings.long: A travelling wave has the form f(x − vt): the same shape, shifted along at speed v. Two of them moving in opposite directions add up to a standing wave.

meanings.short: The mass per unit area of a thin sheet, such as a drum skin.
The mass of a lens per unit area as seen on the sky: all its mass along the line of sight, added up.
How quickly a wave repeats in space: 2π divided by the wavelength, the angle in radians per metre.
meanings.long: Written k, it plays the part for space that angular frequency plays for time. A wave with a large wave number has a short wavelength.

meanings.short: In spectroscopy: one divided by the wavelength, the number of waves per centimetre, used as a measure of energy.
Sending a signal by changing the size of a fast carrier wave in step with the signal, as AM radio does.
meanings.long: The modulated wave is a sum of the carrier and nearby frequencies, so each station needs a band of frequencies around its carrier.

meanings.short: The angle at which light hitting a transparent surface reflects with only one direction of polarization; the other passes in completely.
meanings.long: At this angle the reflected and refracted rays are at right angles, and light polarized in the plane of incidence is not reflected at all. Its tangent is the ratio of the refractive indices.

meanings.short: Different from its own mirror image, as a left hand differs from a right hand.
meanings.long: Chiral molecules, such as sugar, come in left-handed and right-handed forms. A solution of one form turns the polarization of light passing through it.

meanings.short: The sealed end of a pipe, where the air cannot move to and fro but its pressure changes the most.
The end of a pipe open to the room, where the pressure stays at room pressure and the air moves the most.
An end of a string that can slide freely sideways, so the string there stays level and a wave reflects without turning over.
Waves adding so that their crests arrive together, giving a larger wave.
meanings.long: It happens where the waves' paths differ by a whole number of wavelengths, so they arrive in step.

meanings.short: Waves adding so that crests meet troughs, and the waves partly or completely cancel.
meanings.long: It happens where the paths differ by half a wavelength, or by a whole number of wavelengths plus a half.

meanings.short: Two or more oscillating objects joined so that the motion of each pushes on the others.
meanings.long: Their motion looks complicated, but it is a sum of normal modes, in each of which every part oscillates at the same frequency. Two pendulums joined by a spring are the standard example.

meanings.short: A formula that solves a set of linear equations, giving each unknown as a ratio of two determinants.
An idealised spike: zero everywhere except at one point, yet with total area one. It describes a sudden kick or a point source.
meanings.long: The delta function δ(t) is not an ordinary function but is defined by what it does under an integral: integrating f(t)δ(t − a) picks out f(a).

meanings.short: An idealised spike: zero everywhere except at one point, yet with total area one. It describes a sudden kick or a point source.
meanings.long: The delta function δ(t) is not an ordinary function but is defined by what it does under an integral: integrating f(t)δ(t − a) picks out f(a).
meanings.here: A system's response to a delta function is its weight function, and the Laplace transform of the delta function is 1.

meanings.short: A field used inside materials: the electric field plus the effect of the material's lined-up charges, chosen so that Gauss's law counts only free charges.
meanings.long: It is written D = ε₀E + P, with P the polarization. Gauss's law for D counts only free charges, which makes it convenient in matter.

meanings.short: A wave of linked electric and magnetic fields that travels through empty space at the speed of light; light is one.
meanings.long: The two fields are perpendicular to each other and to the direction of travel. Radio, microwaves, light and X-rays are all electromagnetic waves of different wavelengths.

meanings.short: The equation, usually from Newton's second law, that says how a system's position changes with time.
meanings.long: It is usually a differential equation; solving it with the starting position and velocity gives the whole motion.

meanings.short: A way of writing a signal as a sum of pure waves, giving how much of each frequency it contains.
meanings.long: A short pulse needs a wide range of frequencies and a long steady wave only a narrow one; this is the root of the uncertainty principle. In two dimensions it turns an aperture's shape into its diffraction pattern.

meanings.short: A ripple in the shape of space and time, sent out by accelerating masses such as two black holes orbiting each other.
meanings.long: Predicted by general relativity, a gravitational wave stretches space in one direction and squeezes it in the perpendicular one as it passes, by a tiny fraction. It travels at the speed of light.

meanings.short: The rule that certain pairs of quantities, such as a particle's position and momentum, cannot both have exact values at once.
meanings.long: Heisenberg's uncertainty principle says Δx Δp is at least ħ/2. It follows from the wave nature of matter: a wave confined to a small region needs a wide range of wavelengths, just as a short pulse needs a wide range of frequencies. It applies to fields too, so empty space cannot be perfectly smooth.

meanings.short: A supposed extra property, missing from quantum theory, that would decide in advance the outcome of each measurement.
meanings.long: Experiments, such as tests of Bell's inequality, rule out the simple local versions: the chance in quantum mechanics does not seem to come from information we merely lack.

meanings.short: The idea that every point on a wavefront acts as a source of small new waves, whose sum gives the wave further on.
meanings.long: It explains why waves bend round obstacles and spread out after passing through a slit.

meanings.short: A wave in which the medium moves back and forth along the direction the wave travels, as in sound.
meanings.long: In a transverse wave the motion is across the direction of travel instead, as on a plucked string.

meanings.short: A neutron star spinning hundreds of times a second, whose radio beam sweeps past Earth in sharp, clock-like pulses.
meanings.long: It was spun up by matter taken from a companion star. Its pulses are so regular that any spreading between radio frequencies can be measured very precisely.

meanings.short: Lines on a vibrating surface that stay still: the two-dimensional version of the nodes on a string.
A thin strand of glass that guides light along its length by repeated total internal reflection.
How strongly a material responds to a magnetic field, which sets how much field a given current produces in it.
meanings.long: Written μ; in vacuum it is μ₀. Together with the permittivity it fixes the speed of light in the material.

meanings.short: How strongly a material responds to an electric field, which sets how much it weakens the field of charges placed in it.
meanings.long: Written ε; in vacuum it is ε₀. Together with the permeability it fixes the speed of light in the material, and so its refractive index.

meanings.short: How far one oscillation is ahead of another in its cycle, given as an angle.
meanings.long: A phase difference of zero means the two are in step; π (half a cycle) means they are exactly opposite.

meanings.short: A radar made of many fixed emitters whose timing is shifted so their waves add up in a chosen direction, steering the beam without moving.
meanings.long: Changing the phase difference between neighbouring emitters moves the direction of the main peak, so the beam can sweep the sky electronically.

meanings.short: The release of electrons from a metal by light, which happens only above a certain frequency, however bright the light.
meanings.long: Einstein explained it in 1905: light comes in packets (photons) of energy proportional to frequency, and one photon frees one electron.

meanings.short: A wave whose crests are flat, parallel planes, all moving in one direction.
meanings.long: Far from its source, any wave looks like a plane wave over a small region.

meanings.short: A vector giving the direction and rate of energy flow in an electromagnetic field, per unit area.
meanings.long: It is the cross product of the electric and magnetic fields divided by μ₀, measured in watts per square metre.

meanings.short: One of the brightest peaks in the pattern from many slits or sources, where all their waves arrive in step.
The small peaks between the main peaks of a pattern from many slits, where the waves only partly cancel.
A wave whose size, squared, at each place gives the chance of finding the particle there.
meanings.long: In quantum mechanics the wave function is such a wave: the square of its size gives the probability.

meanings.short: A very hot, dense state of matter in which quarks and gluons move freely instead of being bound into protons and neutrons.
meanings.long: It filled the universe for the first few microseconds after the Big Bang, and is made briefly today by colliding heavy nuclei.

meanings.short: A wave plate that delays one direction of the field by a quarter period, turning suitably angled linear polarization into circular.
A thin transparent crystal in which light polarized along one axis travels slower than along the other, shifting their phases.
meanings.long: The phase shift depends on the thickness. A quarter-wave plate shifts by a quarter period, a half-wave plate by half a period.

meanings.short: The direction in a wave plate along which polarized light travels fastest, so it gains the smaller phase delay.
The direction in a wave plate along which polarized light travels slowest, so it gains the larger phase delay.
The direction of a polarizer along which the electric field passes through; the part of the field across it is absorbed.
The basic equation of quantum mechanics, saying how a particle's wave function changes with time.
meanings.long: It plays the part that Newton's second law plays in classical mechanics. Its solutions of fixed energy give the allowed energy levels of atoms.

meanings.short: Replacing sin θ by θ itself, with θ in radians, when the angle is small, which makes many equations much simpler.
meanings.long: For a pendulum it turns the equation of motion into that of simple harmonic motion. The error is about 1 per cent at 14 degrees and smaller below.

meanings.short: The rule linking the angles of a ray before and after it crosses into another material: n₁ sin θ₁ = n₂ sin θ₂.
meanings.long: It follows from matching the waves along the boundary: the wavelength along the surface must be the same on both sides.

meanings.short: How strongly something resists being bent, stretched or squeezed; the greater it is, the stronger the restoring force.
meanings.long: Stiffness gives a restoring force of its own, separate from any tension or gravity. A stiff piano string, for example, makes short waves travel faster than long ones.

meanings.short: The pull along the surface of a liquid or a stretched membrane, per unit length, which tries to make the surface smaller.
The property that a system's laws do not change with time, so a solution started later is still a solution.
meanings.long: It holds when nothing in the equation depends on the time itself. In mechanics it leads to conservation of energy.

meanings.short: Complete reflection of light that tries to leave a dense material, such as glass or water, at too slanting an angle, beyond the critical angle.
meanings.long: Beyond the critical angle Snell's law has no solution for the outgoing ray, so all the light is reflected. Optical fibres rely on it.

meanings.short: The study of light as rays travelling in straight lines, a good picture when the wavelength is very small.
meanings.long: Its two laws are that the angle of reflection equals the angle of incidence and Snell's law of refraction.

meanings.short: The quantity in quantum mechanics whose squared size at each place gives the chance of finding the particle there.
meanings.long: Written ψ, it is in general a complex number at each point. It obeys the Schrödinger equation and holds everything that can be known about the particle.

meanings.short: A short burst of wave made by adding waves of nearby wavelengths, large only in a limited region.
meanings.long: A wave packet moves at the group velocity. The narrower it is, the wider the range of wavelengths it needs, which is the uncertainty principle for waves.

meanings.short: A mass hanging on a coiled spring whose bobbing and twisting are coupled, so its energy passes slowly between the two motions.
An upright metal tube with a heated wire mesh inside, which sings loudly as the rising hot air drives a standing sound wave.
The property of a rule that a sum of inputs gives the sum of their results, and scaling an input scales its result.
meanings.long: A linear map L obeys L(au + bv) = aL(u) + bL(v). Linear equations, determinants (in each row), Lorentz transformations and tensors all have this property, which is what makes superposition work.

meanings.short: The property that sums and multiples of solutions are again solutions, so the responses to separate inputs simply add.
meanings.long: An equation is linear when the unknown and its derivatives appear only to the first power and are not multiplied together. Linearity is what makes the superposition principle work.

meanings.short: Being a straight-line relation: one quantity is simply proportional to the other.
